en: The Practice Method for the Vaipulya Samādhi,
spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui Dynasty,
recorded by his disciple Guanding.

The Esoteric Dharma of Vaipulya Complete with Six Conditions: First, the Esoteric Dharma of Vaipulya: Identifying Obstructions; Second, the Esoteric Dharma of Vaipulya: Prohibitions and Laws; Third, the Esoteric Dharma of Vaipulya: Essential Instructions on Internal Discipline; Fourth, the Esoteric Dharma of Vaipulya: Practice; Fifth, the Esoteric Dharma of Vaipulya: Receiving Precepts; Sixth, [the Conclusion]. Second, the spiritual friend;
third, the preliminary preparations;
fourth, the procurement of robes.
The Fivefold Dharma.
Regarding the six methods of offering, as for the object of the dharma (dharmālambana),
according to the sūtras, there are both general and specific categories.
Regarding the general dharmas:
as at the end of the first fascicle,
they are those practiced by all seven groups of followers.
The essential practice for the seven-day period:
recite the mantras of the three sections.
As the Sūtra says:
At that time, the Chief addressed Gaṅgā, saying:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to hear it..."
"You should abide before that person in a dream and manifest your body.
If that person sees your body,"
One should be taught to practice this true Dharma in this way:
when wishing to practice it, one should observe a fast for seven days.
Bathe three times each day,
put on clean and pure garments,
and sit before an image of the Buddha while holding a five-colored parasol.
When practicing this rite on the eighth or fifteenth day of the month,
even if sentient beings have committed the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), [they shall be purified].
If there were white leprosy on his body that could not be cured or eliminated,
such a thing would be impossible.
If it concerns the twenty-four precepts for bodhisattvas,
the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras,
or the precepts for śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs.
Regarding the precepts for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—
should one violate any one of these various precepts, [one incurs a downfall].
One should repent with single-minded devotion;
that one would not be reborn again is impossible.
Excluding those who lack sincere intent—
this is called the general characteristic of dharmas.
As for what are called the specific characteristics of dharmas:
As stated at the beginning of the fourth fascicle:
the practices and stages for each of the seven classes of followers are distinct,
and their recitation of mantras is likewise distinct.
As it is said in the sutra: "If there is a bhikṣu who has violated the four grave prohibitions,
yet with a sincere mind recollects this dhāraṇī mantra..."
Request one bhikṣu to serve as the presiding master of the repentance ceremony.
Once the mantra has been recited one thousand four hundred times according to the sūtra,
perform one session of repentance.
After eighty-seven days,
having completed the repentance,
these are the roots of all precepts.
If they were not to be reborn,
such a thing would be impossible;
yet if one sees a bhikṣuṇī who has violated the eight grave prohibitions, [it is clear they will be reborn].
If one wishes to extinguish the offenses of the eight grave prohibitions,
one should invite a bhikṣu to serve as the presiding master for confession and practice for ninety-seven days.
Recite the mantra forty-nine times,
then perform one repentance,
following the Master in practice.
It is impossible that these evil karmas would not be eradicated.
If there were a bodhisattva who, having received the eight grave prohibitions, subsequently violated their virtue, [it would be impossible for such karma not to be eliminated].
Recite the mantra six hundred times,
and then perform one confession.
At the time of confession, you should invite a bhikṣu.
Standing before him, he confessed his own sins with his own mouth.
After sixty-seven days had passed,
he experienced in a dream what has been described above.
If even inferior śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs,
upāsakas, or upāsikās should invite a single bhikṣu.
Recite the mantra four hundred times,
and then perform one confession;
continue in this manner until the forty-seventh day has passed.
As stated above,
those who see these two things in a dream should be known as śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerīs.
When upāsakas and upāsikās abide in pure precepts,
this is called the practice of the specific characteristics of the Dharma.
Question: At the end of the first fascicle, it states that the essential core of the seven-day practice is universally applicable to all seven classes of practitioners;
even the ten evil deeds and the five heinous offenses can be eliminated.
For what reason, at the beginning of the fourth fascicle,
are there distinct practices for each day,
with the days being either extended or shortened?
The recitation of the mantra is also distinct.
In response, Mañjuśrī, out of great compassion, again entreated the World-Honored One regarding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
If there are bhikṣus who have committed the four pārājika offenses;
bhikṣuṇīs who have committed the eight pārājika offenses, up to those who have violated the bodhisattva precepts;
as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs.
“If upāsakas and upāsikās violate the grave prohibitions,
how should such offenses as these be extinguished?
The Buddha said:
Because you have asked, I shall now speak.
Had you not asked, I would never have spoken.
Now that it is clear that the methods of repentance differ for each, [I shall explain them].
Since the number of days differs,
we know that the seven-day period for the primary precept is essential;
one must not allow a grave transgression to occur.
One practices this true Dharma.
Why is this? Because the karmic obstructions committed in the present life are particularly grave.
If one does not apply effort and practice,
there is no way to extinguish transgressions;
therefore, the World-Honored One felt compassion for them.
Mañjuśrī inquired:
"In order to rescue the seven classes of followers from the decline and suffering of the hells during the age of turbid evil,
one establishes the distinct characteristics of repentance."
The Method of Eighty-seven Days of Repentance: This method is to be practiced solely by a great bhikṣu. The mantra is as follows:
*Līlavā līlavāde / Kūhakūhāde / Dharālide / Nihārade / Vimālide / Svāhā*. One should recite this while repenting for the four grave prohibitions (*catur-āpatti*).

After one thousand four hundred recitations, perform one repentance. This is the method of repentance for ninety-seven days. This method of repentance for ninety-seven days is to be practiced solely by a great Bhikṣuṇī. The eight prohibitions and mantras for repentance are as follows:

Āre virā kīradate | radate vāmradate | amradate | svāhā. Recite this mantra forty-nine times for each of the eight grave prohibitions (*aṣṭaguru*) as part of the confession. This is the method of confession for sixty-seven days. This practice should be undertaken only by those who have received the Bodhisattva precepts. The mantra is as follows: [Mantra: Āre virā kīradate | radate vāmradate | amradate | svāhā.
*Varale* *kunarale* *kinarale* *ganale ale nale* *atinate atinale* *svāhā*. Recite this mantra six hundred times as a repentance for the eight grave prohibitions (*aṣṭaguru-āpatti*).
This is the method for the forty-seven-day rite of repentance performed after [the initial confession].
This rite is practiced exclusively by śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Furthermore, although the sutra does not explicitly state it, the meaning implies that one should also practice reciting mantras. The mantra is as follows:

*Lokānte muktānte adhimuktānte ugrānte varānta-varṣakānte varṣakānte dūrakṣakānte viśākṣakānte lipakṣakānte varale āle kirale āle cirale āle tilale āle vilāle svāhā*. Having thus repented for the transgression of the grave prohibitions, one should recite this mantra four hundred times and then perform the repentance once; the repentance is to be performed in this manner as described above.
Furthermore, one should request a bhikṣu who is proficient in both the internal and external vinaya— meaning the vinaya of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—
to act as the presiding master for the confession of the two divisions,
monks and nuns; the individual should then personally confess their transgressions.
Before the image, cause them to hear and understand the requested objective as explained in the sūtra,
according to the ritual of the *maṇḍala*.
Regarding clothing, ritual implements,
maintaining purity, and bathing,
follow the seven-day practice method exactly, without seeking signs from the King of Dreams.
There is no limit to the number of people;
there is also no fixed rule for entering the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*).
As soon as one is able to prepare, one should proceed.
If there are practitioners who examine the scriptural texts themselves,
they will find that what has been transgressed as described above is not recorded here in this abbreviated version.
Having performed each of these individually,
one may then perform the foremost repentance,
the Seven-Day Essential Heart Repentance Method, also known as the General Repentance Method. The mantra is as follows:

Namo urugāya citte jināgata-mi svāhā. Tadyathā: pūjilambe upatāpye pūjilambe lepara anutātadyathā budhyudaye pūrṇajīve svāhā. Namo mahāpūtāpe. Namo mahālipūtāhe. Namo puṣpasaṃcayadhāraṇyai. Piśāca-ṭṭhi-ukāvana taṭṭāvana gaṅgāvana tagaṅge āle nāle nārāle svāhā. This mantra must not be used for treating illnesses.
Furthermore, regarding the second [condition] for what is sought— the condition of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)—
there are three types.
The first is the spiritual friend as external protector (bāhyarakṣaka-kalyāṇamitra).
That which is called being able to shoulder all matters and provide what is required;
protecting and guiding practitioners by means of wholesome deeds,
just as a compassionate mother nurtures and protects her infant.
First, do not allow those who practice to have any discursive thoughts.
Second, associate with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) who are practitioners of long-standing experience on the Path.
Traveling together on the same path,
they mutually exhort one another to abandon the notions of "self," "other," and "person.
If they see a fellow practitioner giving rise to thoughts of transgression toward sentient beings, [they should intervene].
One should immediately give rise to a heart of compassion and instruct them according to the Dharma,
just as when a person's head or clothing is set ablaze by fire,
one must rescue them and cause the fire to be extinguished quickly.
If one has not extinguished the mind, one cannot attain peace;
it is just as if one's own body were harmed by poison,
such that no other thought remains.
It is solely for the benefit and peace of practitioners,
to nourish the Dharma-body and to encourage diligent cultivation;
it skillfully reconciles disputes so that they blend like water and milk.
Just as gain and loss are shared by those on the same ship,
so it is with the practitioner:
they encourage others to hear what they have not heard before, and together they attain the nectar of immortality.
Riding the boat of skillful means, one reaches the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Regarding the third type of spiritual friend who provides instruction:
it refers to one who has long practiced the path and whose practice is clear and distinct.
Sealed by the Victorious One,
he understands the characteristics of the inner and outer vinayas;
he recognizes prohibitions and obstacles, and knows where there is penetration and where there is blockage.
I respectfully request you to serve as the presiding master of this ritual site.
I shall welcome you at your arrival and see you off at your departure, prostrating three times each day,
and provide offerings of food and drink of a hundred flavors.
One should regard this person as a king of physicians;
one should regard one's own body as a festering ulcer;
and one should regard this person as a deva.
One should regard one's own body as the three evil realms;
one should regard such a person as a bridge;
and one should regard one's own body as being in the midst of drowning.
One should regard this person as being on the correct path,
regard one's own self as being lost,
and regard this person as one who has reached the land of peace and happiness.
One should regard one's own body as a prisoner in a prison;
by giving rise to a sense of profound urgency,
all offenses that obstruct the Path shall be extinguished.
If one does not possess such a person as described above,
it is sufficient that the root of one's precepts be pure and protected by the life-preserving bag.

Although they may not be able to speak with eloquence or provide extensive clarification of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they may also serve as secondary spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). 3.
Regarding the three conditions for the preliminary preparations (*pūrvaprayoga*): as for the three conditions for the preliminary preparations...
Practice the Way for seven days;
recite mantras to bring about efficacy,
and perform prostrations and repentance with utmost sincerity.
I pray to the twelve Dream Kings,
seeking to behold their forms and characteristics;
if I am moved by even a single one of these signs, [may my wish be fulfilled].
Only then can one perform such a method of repentance.
As the Sūtra says:
"If there are men or women..."
Within that dream, they cultivate supernormal powers and are able to fly;
silken banners and canopies hang suspended behind this person.
Such is what is seen.
This is called the *cūḍāmaṇi*.
If any man or woman, within their dreams, should see an image, a relic, a stūpa, a temple, or an assembly of the great Saṃgha—
those who see such things [shall attain this].
This is Jīvala. If there are men or women who,
within their dreams, see a king or a minister.
One who is seen wearing clean, pure garments and riding alone on a white horse is Maucilinda.
If there are men or women who,
within their dreams, see themselves riding an elephant across a great river—
those who see such a vision.
This is Kankhala.
If there are men or women who,
in their dreams, ride upon a camel to a high mountain;
One who sees in this manner perceives these five signs above the Multitude Forest (Bahuputraka);
these are the signs of a householder.
If there is a bhikṣu who seeks this Dharma, he shall,
even within a dream, ascend a high seat and turn the wheel of the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who sees in this way is indeed a Vāriṇīra.
If there is a bhikṣu...
Within that dream, he arrived at the foot of a tree and ascended it to receive full ordination upon a precept platform;
such was what he saw.
This is the *Dānalina* [sūtra].
If there is a bhikṣu who,
within his dreams, sits before an image of the Buddha.
To invite the assembly of monks and provide them with offerings—
those who see it in this way are the Cāndana-ārāmas.
If there is a bhikṣu who,
within a dream, sees a tree with flowers and fruits in full bloom,
and enters into dhyāna-samādhi beneath that tree.
One who perceives in this way possesses the four characteristics mentioned above, namely those of a forest-dwelling bhikṣu;
these are the characteristics of a renunciant bhikṣu.
If there is a great king who,
within his dreams, travels in the four directions carrying a sword,
and sees such a thing as this:
This is the Kalinga; this is the mark of a king.
If there is a high minister who, in his dreams, sees various people...
Having bathed his body with various water jars,
having applied various fragrances and put on clean garments—
seeing him thus.
This is the mark of a great minister:
if there is a queen who,
in her dreams, mounts a white ram and enters deep water.
Within that water there are various venomous snakes;
seeing such things is the omen for the king, his ministers, and his consort of this kingdom, Pāṭaliputra.
Question: The sūtra merely states that these are the marks of a lady;
on what basis can it be known that these are the marks of a king’s great minister’s wife?
Answer: In the first five characteristics mentioned above,
it refers only to men and women.
This includes all laypeople without exception;
however, the sūtra further explains the characteristics of kings and ministers separately.
Thus, we know that he is not included among the aforementioned men.

Since this sutra specifically mentions "the consort" (*bhāryā*), it is logically clear that she is not included among the aforementioned women; rather, she is the consort of a king or a high minister.
Furthermore, since the wife has already been mentioned separately,
it should be treated in the same way here as well.
Moreover, regarding these twelve dreams, such as the *jantāka* and so forth:
Thereupon, the Māra King resolved his mind to protect and assist those who receive and uphold this Great Vaipulya Dhāraṇī;
he is indeed a Mahāsattva.
To one who perceives in this manner, one may then explain the practice for the seven-day journey.
4. The Circumstances Concerning the Preparation of Robes:
Both those who have left the household life and those who remain at home must possess three types of robes.
All must be new and clean;
if there are no new ones,
wash the old ones until they are clean.
One should bathe him with fragrant water.
Furthermore, one may use a cloth garment as an upper robe if his three robes are not complete.
One should invite a monk who knows the Dharma to perform the confession for the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense,
and one should properly receive and maintain the three robes and six requisites according to the Dharma.
Even down to the offense of *duṣkṛta*,
all must be confessed;
only then will the practice be perfected.
Regarding the three kinds of pure robes mentioned above:
the most superior pure one is intended for wearing while entering the *maṇḍala*.
One robe is for intermediate purification,
intended to be worn when proceeding from the bathing area toward the place of practice;
one robe is intended to be worn at all times during sitting and rising.
Question: Regarding the three robes of a householder,
are these secular garments or are they the robes of one who has left the household life?
The answer is that the Sūtra states:

"One is the robe for those who have left the household life, which is distinguished by being sewn with single seams; this robe is intended to be worn when entering the Dharma hall, following the ritual protocol of the Buddhas of the three periods."
Although one wears the robes of a renunciant,
one should not shave the hair; furthermore,
one must possess a tooth-stick, cleansing powder, a water flask, eating utensils, and a sitting mat.
As is the rule for bhikṣus,
he shall be led to the place of practice;
the other two garments are those of a layperson.
Proceed according to the same method as before.
Furthermore, one must prepare a pair of soft, fine leather sandals in two sizes.
Additionally, it is necessary to construct two new latrines, one large and one small.
Parting from the Former Precepts.
5. The Conditions for the Fivefold Dharma Practice. Regarding the conditions for the fivefold dharma practice:
on the eighth and fifteenth days of the month, one may enter the *dōjō*.
The number of practitioners may at most reach ten people before returning;
it should not exceed this number,
as doing so would contravene the teachings.
If there are many practitioners, one must separately construct a ritual site (maṇḍala).
It should be made as a circular altar,
measuring sixteen feet in both length and breadth.
Smeared the ground with fragrant mud and placed a high seat upon it;
he then invited the twenty-four images along with their seats.
Each is one chi high.
There are twenty-four silk banners and one ancient mirror to consecrate the ritual site.
Construct a circular canopy of five colors and suspend it above the altar.
The practitioner may prepare a low-legged bench measuring five *cun* and sit facing the Buddha.
The felt rugs, mats, and cushions must all be new and clean.
Adorn the *maṇḍala* with the finest treasures and wonders of the world,
and perform offerings according to the Dharma by burning incense and scattering flowers.
Every day he swept and sprinkled the ground,
and constantly kept a basin filled with various types of incense— such as frankincense, storax, aloeswood, powdered incense,
and island-shore sandalwood— as well as fragrant water.
Upon the wooden board, one washes away impurities and enters the inner purity.
One removes old clothes and leather sandals, placing them far outside;
one must enter the inner purity wearing fresh, clean garments.
Do not allow pure contact to become mixed with the impure.
6. Regarding the six conditions for making offerings:
these should be prepared according to one's capacity.
All varieties of food and drink, as well as all utensils, must be purified with fragrant water.
Since it may be impossible to find such provisions in mountainous regions or remote places,
one must perform at least one offering on the first day.
When the seven days have passed, perform one offering.
On the day of concluding the ritual site (maṇḍala),
invite the assembly of monks, with no limit on their number.
It is without hindrance to act according to one's capacity and strength.
If one can extensively establish the two fields of compassion and reverence, it will be of the greatest benefit.
If there is a donor who makes offerings every day, [it is likewise beneficial].
Therefore, it is necessary to provide separate provisions for whatever is required.
Second, regarding the four ways of removing obstacles to consciousness and achieving composure: first, bathing to achieve composure.
Second, moderation in food and drink;
third, moderation in walking practice;
fourth, moderation in sitting meditation. Regarding moderation in bathing: as for "moderation in bathing":
The practice for the three periods of the day is regulated:

sees their own form emaciated and wearing soiled, greasy clothes;
Furthermore, seeing those riding broken-down carts in fear of falling off,
they become sorrowful;
or they see their bodies naked, without a single thread of clothing, and utterly ruined.
It should be known that this manifests as the appearance of the third category of precept transgression.
If, while walking, sitting, or even in a dream,
a practitioner sees a broken bowl, an empty vessel, or black clothing;
If one sees them consuming wine or other fermented liquors at improper times,
or pushing and shoving one another,
it should be known that the signs of an offense against the ninety rules of the third category are manifest.
If, while walking, sitting, or even in dreams,
the practitioner perceives all objective spheres as dim and unable to be clear and pure;
if the mind finds no joy and the body feels heavy, such that one finds no flavor in the practices one undertakes.
It should be known that this constitutes an offense against the fourth category, the *pātayantika* (提舍尼) precepts,
as well as the preliminary and subsequent preparatory stages (*pūrvāparaprayoga*),
and the manifestation of the characteristics of breaking the precepts within the six and seven groups of offenses.
Regarding the manifestation of auspicious signs:
if one sees an inauspicious sign, one should repent with a sincere heart;
once the sin of violating the precepts has been extinguished, the auspicious sign will immediately appear.
Now, one who wishes to cultivate the path and receive the Dharma must first purify their precepts;
if the precepts are pure, the Dharma will flourish.
The signs of their respective lightness and gravity will all appear before them.
If, while dreaming or while walking or sitting,
the practitioner sees themselves wearing a jeweled crown upon their head;
His body is adorned with necklaces and his physical marks are subtle and wondrous;
one should know that this is the manifestation of the sign of the purity of the precepts, the first chapter of the practitioner’s repentance.
If a practitioner, whether in a dream or while walking or sitting,
sees a jeweled garland upon the crown of their head,
or sees a handsome person with all faculties complete;
It should be known that when the signs of the second purification of precepts through repentance manifest, whether in dreams or while walking or sitting,
one may see fine, smooth, thin garments,
or see people who are well-adorned and disciplined.
Holding the robes and alms bowl with pure deportment,
one should know that this is the manifestation of the sign of purity for the practitioner’s repentance of the third category of precepts.
Whether in dreams or while walking and sitting, the practitioner—
If one sees whole vessels and bright white-colored robes,
indicating the harmony of the Sangha's affairs;
or if one sees pure food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha.
It should be known that when a practitioner’s third category of ninety precepts has been purified through repentance,
signs of this purity will appear. Whether in dreams or while walking or sitting,
the practitioner will personally perceive their body as supple and their movements as light and agile.
When the mind feels joy toward the dharmas one has studied,
it should be known that for the practitioner, the signs of purification regarding the fourth category of precepts,
as well as the preparatory stages before and after, have appeared.
The sixth and seventh precepts manifest the signs of purity.
This provides a brief indication of the five chapters that distinguish the characteristics of good and evil.
The detailed particulars therein cannot be recorded in writing unless one has personally realized them through practice and received oral instructions.
2. Clarifying the Extinction or Non-extinction of the Ten Evil and Ten Wholesome Karmas. Regarding the clarification of the extinction or non-extinction of the ten evil and ten wholesome karmas:
although the characteristics of a practitioner's karma are indeed numerous, [the essential nature remains consistent].
They do not go beyond the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome deeds.
Because the practitioner relies on the power of repentance,
all of them manifest before him.
Regarding the ten unwholesome actions:
if a practitioner, whether in a dream or while walking or sitting,
perceives objects that are coarse and evil.
The multitude, wielding blades and staves, slaughtered one another;
some saw humans or animals coming to claim their lives,
while others saw [enemies] cutting off their paths and reviling them with anger.
Or if one sees many sick people with short lifespans,
one should know that this is a manifestation of the karmic sign of killing;
such occurs for the practitioner within a dream.
If one sees dregs, refuse, or filthy garments and ornaments;
or sees various clothes and precious objects lying at one's feet;
or sees granaries and storehouses in ruins.
Alternatively, one may see oneself in a desolate and terrifying place within a black mountain cave;
or see a poor person approaching;
or see oneself burdened by another's debt.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the karmic signs of stealing.
If, while dreaming or while walking or sitting,
a practitioner sees a great mountain or rock formation, blue in color, crumbling and collapsing.
The roads were blocked and cut off;
some saw vast, overflowing floods,
while others saw defiled objects that overwhelmed their chests.
They are obstructed and cannot pass through;
or upon seeing an object of perception, they immediately give rise to a defiled mind;
or they see their kinsmen acting contrary to the Dharma.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the signs of sensual desire.
Whether in dreams or while walking and sitting,
if the practitioner sees coarse and evil things, [this is the sign].
They slander one another;
some are deceived by others and lose their way on the correct path.
Though they possess reason themselves, their grievances are suppressed and cannot be voiced.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the karmic sign of false speech.
If, while dreaming or while walking or sitting,
the practitioner sees two mountains obstructing the way so that sounds and messages cannot pass through;
Or if one sees friends and relatives separated or family members in discord,
one should know that this is a manifestation of the mark of double-tongued speech.
Whether in dreams or while walking and sitting, the practitioner [should recognize this].
If one hears the sound of a terrible roar,
the mind is filled with fear and finds no place to rest;
or if one sees someone reviling them with insults.
"You have deceived me; I now requite you.
Or, when one sees people engaging in mutual strife and contention, one should know that this is the manifestation of evil verbal abuse.
If, while walking, sitting, or even in dreams,
the practitioner sees their exhaled breath exiting the mouth like dregs,
or sees their own mouth speaking with stammering and obstruction so that words do not come forth;
If one’s speech and words are not clearly understood,
and others do not believe or accept what one tells them,
know that this is the manifestation of the karmic characteristic of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
If a practitioner, whether in a dream or while walking or sitting,
sees clouds arising like a black wind,
or sees those with great desire who are greedily attached to karmic rewards;
If one sees the five sensory objects appearing in front in a state of chaotic confusion,
or if one sees oneself sinking and unable to emerge,
one should know that these are the manifestations of the signs of lustful desire.
If a practitioner, whether in a dream or while walking or sitting,
sees mountains of the seven treasures shrouded by clouds and mist,
which then transform into earth and stone;
Fear arises in the mind;
or one sees someone brandishing their hand to strike or beat them with resentment and rage;
or one sees someone coming to cause disturbance and affliction.
Or one may see someone come and pull at one's clothes to take them away,
yet one repents and apologizes without letting go;
or one may see venomous snakes covering the ground, spitting poison toward people.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the sign of hatred.
Whether in a dream or while walking or sitting,
if the practitioner sees various sand, gravel, and stones scattering and defiling them, [this is the sign].
If one sees the objects before them covered by dark clouds approaching like a veil of gloom,
the practitioner’s mental path becomes obscured and blocked, such that they do not know where it leads;
or one may see black elephants crossing back and forth.
Or they see people from border regions who do not believe in the Triple Gem,
whose minds are filled with flattery, crookedness, and hesitation;
or they see those who have fallen away from their precepts and returned to secular life.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the signs of wrong view.
Herein, ten types of coarse matters are briefly set forth as the manifestations of the signs of the ten non-virtuous actions.
If a practitioner, having seen such evils as these,
can repent with a sincere heart,
the ten evil karmas will be extinguished.
At that time, auspicious signs appear spontaneously.
If the practitioner sees black colors transform into white and yellow,
sentient beings will gaze at one another with hearts full of joy, respect, and love, never wearying of it.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the sign of the extinction of the karma of killing through confession.
If one sees jewel trees fully endowed with flowers and fruits,
or sees various wealth and goods, [this is likewise a sign].
When people mutually present gifts to one another,
you should know that this is the manifestation of the sign that the karma of stealing has been extinguished through repentance.
If one sees lotus flowers filling Jambudvīpa, [this likewise indicates the same].
Alternatively, one may see all people born through transformation from lotuses,
or see the person before one preaching the pure and white Dharma;
one should know that these are signs appearing as the karma of lust is extinguished through repentance.
If one sees someone showing a city of the seven treasures,
and within that city people show him exquisite halls and residences,
his heart will rejoice; yet he turns his face toward another direction and sees it again.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the sign of the extinction of the karma of false speech.
If the practitioner sees a multitude gathered together discussing harmonious and lawful matters,
or a joyful assembly celebrating and delighting in festivities;
One should know that these are signs of the manifestation of the extinction of the karmic offenses of divisive speech through repentance.
If one sees a great road that is clean and pure,
or sees travelers returning from afar and greets them with a heart of compassion, [these are likewise signs].
Whether they perceive them as their father or mother,
or hear sounds praising the Triple Gem,
you should know that these are signs appearing that the karma of abusive speech is being extinguished.
If a practitioner sees a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) exhorting them to diligence and preaching the essential points of the true Dharma, they will give rise to faith and joy,
practicing according to what has been taught.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the signs of the extinction of the karma of frivolous speech.
If the practitioner sees his body undergoing great suffering and distress,
he will suddenly awaken himself to this truth.
All these are reckoned as body and mind,
which constitute the root of manifold sufferings;
the bones and joints are false and provisional, inhabited by various kinds of worms.
He sees his own body as if the entire great hell were ablaze with fire,
burning it away until nothing remains.
One should know that this is the manifestation of the sign of the cessation of the karma of sensual desire.
If the practitioner sees all emaciated sentient beings transformed into those who are handsome and facing one another with serene countenances, [he knows this is the sign].
When the heavens open and the sun appears, illuminating all with light,
or when one sees withered trees flourishing in vigor,
one should know that these are signs of the extinction of the karma of anger.
If a practitioner sees a wish-fulfilling jewel raining down all manner of treasures, which sentient beings gather and use without exhaustion;
or if they see a bhikṣu holding an alms bowl, and a sense of affectionate joy arises in their heart.
Or one may see a bhikṣu preaching the sublime Dharma and summoning them to enter samādhi together;
one should know that this is a manifestation of the signs of the extinction of the karma of wrong views.
This is truly because the practitioner’s merit from repentance has been perfected, and the signs of the ten wholesome actions have already manifested in immeasurable ways;
how much more so the hundreds of thousands of myriads of varieties of manifestations therein, which cannot be fully described.
Question: The characteristics [of meditative objects] are immeasurable,
and the practices of the practitioners differ from one another.
The attainment of the Dharma is also different.
In what way are they of one kind?
The answer is:
The initial statement provides a brief indication,
enabling the practitioner to know that such states exist within the path of practice;
it directly clarifies the characteristics of transgressions regarding one precept among the five categories and its seven branches.
It arises conditioned by greed,
or it arises conditioned by hatred,
or it arises conditioned by delusion.
There are twenty-one aspects of transgression and twenty-one aspects of upholding;
these are likewise twenty-one from the very moment one first receives the precepts.
Beginning from the Avīci Hell and extending upward to the body of the Buddha,
throughout the sentient and insentient beings of the trichiliocosm,
all give rise to the unconditioned precepts (*anabhisaṃskāra-śīla*).
Based on a single precept, the instances of observance and transgression are manifold;
even across the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, they are unspeakable and incalculable, as vast as infinite atoms.
Thus, the characteristics of observance and transgression are likewise boundless.
Whether manifesting through signs or appearing through manifestations,
these cannot be recorded in writing.

Since both self and others have been clarified,

Why is this? Because characteristics differ from one another; they vary in their concealment or manifestation, and in their degree of gravity. The mind [responds] accordingly.

A question is asked:
"The true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) possesses no characteristics of good or evil."
Question: How is it that while practicing the true dharma of all Buddhas, there is the manifestation of signs? Answer:
The true mark of all dharmas is signless.
It can demonstrate the characteristics of the world.
When a practitioner walks the path, they do not dwell on characteristics nor dwell on the absence of characteristics;
they simply contemplate the true nature of the mind.
When the mind is pure, all phenomena are pure;
when the mind is exhausted, all phenomena are exhausted.
It is simply that as the mind and mind-states successively increase in power, their perfected characteristics manifest.
It is like a water basin placed in a sealed room;
although there is no mental discrimination, various images appear of their own accord.
It is asked:
When signs appear, it is difficult to distinguish between the true and the false.
How, then, can one discern them in order to accept or reject?
The answer is:
It is truly difficult to distinguish between the authentic and the false.
Even if a good spiritual friend makes a definitive judgment for you,
nevertheless, the practitioner must not grasp at any signs whatsoever during the four modes of conduct.
One must not abandon it.
If one contemplates through mental recollection and observation, one can perceive Prajñā;
yet to grasp it would be like a person grasping at empty space.
If one relinquishes it as a person relinquishes space,
the equal dharma-realm is likewise so.
